bib.title: Can Large Language Models Explain Themselves? A Study of LLM-Generated Self-Explanations

question: How faithful are the feature-attribution self-explanations ChatGPT generates for sentiment predictions, compared with occlusion and LIME?
contributions: First rigorous assessment of an LLM's ability to self-generate feature attribution explanations (full per-word and top-k), generated explain-then-predict and predict-and-explain
Comparison with occlusion and LIME on five faithfulness metrics and Krishna et al. agreement metrics
Finding that model predictions and attribution values are heavily rounded and insensitive to word removal, limiting evaluation power

method.summary: ChatGPT is prompted zero-shot to output a sentiment label, a confidence and a per-word importance list (or top-3 words), either before (E-P) or after (P-E) the prediction. Occlusion and LIME are computed on the same prompted model using the confidence number as the prediction, and all are scored with faithfulness and agreement metrics.

datasets.name: Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST)
datasets.split: random subset of the test set; labels binarised at 0.5
datasets.preprocessing: words removed by deletion for partial inputs

inference.samples: one generation per input; no repeated runs or seeds reported; random tie-breaking among equal saliency values during evaluation
inference.prompting: zero-shot system prompts (Tables I, II, IV, V) asking for Python list of (word, importance in [-1,1]) tuples plus (class, confidence); top-k variants ask for top 3 words; few-shot tried but not used

parameters.top_k: min(1, floor(L/5)) as printed, L = words in sentence (Table IV/V prompts show top 3); likely a typo for max
parameters.LIME perturbations: 10 x number of tokens, average 183 per explanation (lime default 5,000)
parameters.experiment time: about half an hour per full set of experiments on one instance

other.prediction: decimal confidence in the model's text output used as f(x); logits not available

metrics.name: Comp (comprehensiveness)
metrics.definition: drop in prediction when the top-ranked words are removed, per Zhou and Shah

metrics.name: Suff (sufficiency)
metrics.definition: drop in prediction when only the top-ranked words are kept

metrics.name: DFMIT
metrics.definition: decision flip rate on removing most important token

metrics.name: DFFrac
metrics.definition: minimum fraction of tokens to remove to flip decision

metrics.name: RankDel
metrics.definition: rank correlation with model prediction after word deletion

metrics.name: Comp@k, Suff@k, DFMIT@k
metrics.definition: top-k versions with k words removed or kept together

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: classification accuracy against binarised SST labels

metrics.name: Agreement metrics
metrics.definition: pairwise rank agreement, rank correlation, rank agreement, sign agreement, signed rank agreement, feature agreement, IoU, from Krishna et al.

eval.protocol: Each of E-P and P-E treated as a separate model; occlusion and LIME computed under the same system prompt; single pass over 100 sentences; no significance tests.

prompts.text: You are a creative and intelligent movie review analyst, whose purpose is to aid in sentiment analysis of movie reviews. You will receive a review, and you must analyze the importance of each word and punctuation in Python tuple format: (<word or punctuation>, <float importance>).

limits: Single model (ChatGPT, version unstated), single task (SST sentiment), single explanation type, 100 sentences, no repeated runs or significance tests
Prediction is the stated confidence number, not token probabilities, and is rounded and insensitive to word removal, so metrics may lack discriminative power
Top-k explanations come from a differently-prompted model, not the E-P/P-E models
No human study of understandability; no retraining-based faithfulness evaluation; few-shot prompting abandoned due to memorisation
Top-k formula printed as min(1, floor(L/5)), inconsistent with top 3 in prompts
